This paper introduces and evaluates several novel approaches to transform the typical multi-period portfolio optimization challenge into sequential decision problems. The primary advantage of this transformation lies in the ability to solve it dynamically with relative ease using dynamic programming. However, these methods remain susceptible to the "curse of dimensionality." To address this, we also propose solutions that bypass this limitation. Our proposals are validated through numerical examples and a comprehensive empirical analysis based on daily data spanning twenty years for a distinct set of assets. The results demonstrate that the suggested approaches effectively resolve the issue of overfitting that plagues portfolio optimization when historical data is utilized for optimization. Furthermore, we investigate and present evidence regarding the feasibility of simplifying the multi-period optimization problem into a single-period task, ultimately showing that linear programming remains a viable solution even when the number of financial instruments exceeds the count of available historical data points. Evidently, financial institutions with access to extensive historical data can significantly enhance their portfolio optimization outcomes by leveraging our methods. Additionally, these techniques can be readily adapted to a wide range of financial instruments, including cryptocurrencies. We provide an open-source implementation of our approach at https://github.com/erik-rued/quasiop.

This paper introduces a novel bidirectional attention mechanism (BiAM) that utilizes a multi-modal learning approach to jointly train the bottom layers of an ASR encoder and a text encoder. In a single-task scenario on the Librispeech corpus, the dual-encoder model achieved a WER reduction of 25.85% (from 4.44% to 3.26%) compared to baseline models. We demonstrate that, conditionally on the random matrix $H$, the lattice points form independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) complex random variables that converge to the Gaussian Unitary Ensemble (GUE) within a specific regime. This result establishes the first instance of GUE behavior on an infinite lattice. A significant implication of this finding is the convergence to the discrete GUE determinant process, which serves as the foundation for our main result. As a preliminary step toward understanding the asymptotic behavior of $H$ for large lattice sizes, we analyze the statistics of specific sites, such as those located on the axes. Specifically, we prove that variables on the "bottom cut" are mutually independent and converge to the circular law, while those on the "right cut" also converge to the circular law, conditional on their neighbors to the left. Furthermore, we show that variables immediately adjacent to the cuts are independent of those directly opposite the cuts and follow the GUE distribution. These discoveries collectively offer a rigorous justification for the emergence of the GUE determinant process across the remainder of the lattice. Large $N$ results are relevant to various fields, including random tilings, the discrete Korteweg-de Vries equation, and the random matrix Dyson Brownian motion at time $t=1$. We report experimental data from NbN nanowires that not only exhibit this critical voltage but also demonstrate its tunability via a side-gate electrode, which induces periodic variations in the critical voltage. Although these findings align qualitatively with predictions regarding quantum interference of phase slip events, the observed tuning periodicity exceeds simple band-structure expectations by two orders of magnitude and matches the voltage across a Josephson contact deposited on the nanowire side electrodes. Video prediction represents a significant challenge in computer vision, particularly when predicting novel view videos from multiple available cross-view recordings. Existing methods often struggle with noise inherent in multi-view cross-attribution and fail to balance the use of these features effectively. To address this, we propose a novel strategy for noise reduction and optimization that enables more effective learning from multi-view data. Specifically, our method learns the optimization of novel view features from multi-view cross-attribution representations using spherical linear interpolation (SLIP) across spatial coordinates. Additionally, we have integrated this approach with optimization layers for both frame and optical flow. Experimental findings indicate that the proposed method surpasses state-of-the-art results. The source code is available online. **Our cross-attribution network is open-source and hosted on GitHub:** https://github.com/hamzehamzeh/CATNVP.

Cross-viewing is a crucial task in video analysis, particularly for surveillance, where it involves predicting a target video from multiple source videos. However, existing methods often rely on simple concatenation or averaging of multi-view features, which can be noisy and lead to suboptimal performance. To overcome this, we introduce a new network architecture capable of accurately estimating novel view features from multi-view cross-attribution. By representing these multi-view features in a spatial coordinate system, we apply spherical linear interpolation (SLIP) to synthesize the desired novel view features. This approach, titled CATNVP, offers several advantages: it is cross-domain robust, requires no training data, and is computationally efficient. Experimental results show that our method exceeds state-of-the-art performance. The source code is open-source and can be found on GitHub.

Since its emergence in late 2019, the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic has posed a formidable global challenge. Originating in Wuhan, China, the virus rapidly disseminated to other Asian nations and subsequently to worldwide populations. As of May 2021, approximately 178 million infections and over 3 million deaths have been recorded across 220 countries and regions. While genomic sequencing has enabled the identification and tracking of viral lineages and variants, the precise mechanisms driving transmission rates and the relative contributions of different pathways remain subjects of intense debate. This uncertainty hinders the calibration of key model parameters and complicates the development of effective mitigation and vaccination strategies. Although contact tracing remains a primary method for estimating contact rates and driving contact tracing algorithms, it effectively captures only infections resulting from close, face-to-face interactions, failing to account for transmission via shared environments, common surfaces, or contaminated objects—modes that were particularly significant during the early stages of the outbreak.

We introduce a straightforward method for calculating an upper bound of the Lipschitz constant across various $p$-norms for feedforward neural networks comprising standard layer types. This approach allows us to frame the training of a neural network with a bounded Lipschitz constant as a constrained optimization problem, solvable via projected stochastic gradient methods. ) for quantifying peripheral blood volume (PBV) and plasma protein binding (PPB) with polymeric therapeutics presents substantial difficulties. These polymeric agents possess a high molecular weight, resulting in a non-point spread distribution that significantly complicates PET imaging quantification. Specifically, the large size of the precursors impedes efficient plasma-cell separation, causing red blood cells to remain contaminated with substantial amounts of unlabeled polymer. Furthermore, the substantial unlabeled plasma concentration creates a substantial scatter source that degrades both the raw data and reconstructed images. Contaminated red blood cells also obscure the tissue background, complicating plasma region definition and potentially leading to overestimation of PPB. Additionally, kinetic modeling becomes further compromised by errors in plasma input function calculation due to these issues. This study demonstrates these problems through contaminated red blood cell images and an exaggerated PET scatter component in both raw data and reconstructed images. We show that even minor inaccuracies in plasma activity concentration—such as a 5% overestimation—can cause significant discrepancies in area under the curve (AUC) estimates, impacting decisions regarding PBV and PPB. To mitigate these challenges, we evaluated several image processing strategies, including various scatter correction methods and contaminated blood ROI definition techniques. Our findings indicate that an external scatter correction method, specifically the step and shoot approach, effectively reduces scatter in the image center without increasing noise in the background. Moreover, defining the ROI as a circle with a 10 mm diameter minimizes overestimation of PPB. Collectively, these approaches reduce inaccuracies in the plasma input function, thereby lowering errors in PPB and AUC estimates. Despite these improvements, the method still struggles to fully eliminate scatter in images containing a significant unlabeled precursor concentration. Ultimately, careful technical execution and validation against small molecule and low molecular weight antibody standards are essential to ensure the reliability of these measurements. These results may prove valuable in optimizing the design of subsequent in vivo polymeric therapeutic studies.

This study explores the relationship between Centering Theory and contemporary coreference resolution systems. We propose an operational definition of centering and employ a search-based methodology to systematically evaluate whether neural coreference resolvers comply with CT rules through various discourse metrics. Our information-theoretic analysis indicates a positive correlation between coreference and centering, yet demonstrates that high-performing neural resolvers gain little advantage from explicitly modeling centering concepts. Furthermore, we find that contextualized embeddings encapsulate much of the necessary coherence information, explaining why CT yields minimal improvements for modern neural systems utilizing pretrained representations. Finally, we address coreference factors unmodeled by standard CT, such as world knowledge and recency bias. By formulating an enhanced version of CT that incorporates recency, we show it captures coreference information more effectively than the original formulation. We release both the enhanced centering classifier and our experimental setup for coreference resolution, enabling future research into utterance-level coreference modeling. Our findings suggest that a recency-aware centering signal better represents local coreference distribution than traditional centering features alone. Consequently, integrating a modern recency model with contemporary neural resolvers could potentially surpass current state-of-the-art results.

### 1. Introduction

Coreference is a fundamental linguistic phenomenon where an expression denotes the same entity as another (Grefenstette et alel, 2019). For instance, in the sentence "The dog barked. It was loud," the pronoun "it" refers to "the dog." Accurately identifying such coreferent expressions is essential for natural language understanding (Chen et al., 2016; Li et al., 2020). Although neural methods have significantly boosted sentence-level sentence evaluation (F1), they continue to underperform on long-document coreference tasks (Gordon et al., 2021). This paper investigates the role of Centering Theory (CT; Grosz et al., 1995) in utterance-level coreference evaluation. We document that CT underutilizes information for this purpose, release an updated model, and demonstrate that this enhancement better captures coreference patterns than standard CT.

We attempted to synthesize a one-year ASM from a short-exposure, one-week observation dataset using three ML-based deconvolution techniques: standard convolution, non-negative matrix factorization (NNMF), and a machine-unlearning technique. The ML unlearning approach involved training a model on the full one-year dataset and then exposing it to the actual one-week data for prediction. To evaluate the accuracy of the learned models, we compared the input and output data using a loss function, and we assessed the ML model's performance based on the difference between these evaluations. Our findings indicate that the ML learning and unlearning methods are effective for deriving a one-week ASM from a one-year dataset. Specifically, the unlearning methods of both standard convolution and NNMF yielded higher image quality than the conventional learning method, with the NNMF method showing superior results in reducing point spread function (PSF) smearing and photon pile-up effects, alongside more accurate background subtraction. These findings suggest that ASMs can be learned from datasets five orders of magnitude smaller than what is required for routine observation. Consequently, this method could enable the real-time monitoring of ASMs across the entire sky with a temporal resolution far exceeding the current limits. Such capabilities would be invaluable for identifying new Variable Energy Phenomena (VEPs), which have the potential to advance astrophysics and cosmology. Additionally, this technique is applicable to improving learning from small datasets in general, even when the specific object or phenomenon under investigation is unknown.

In this setting, machines arrive online and must be assigned to identical, unrelated, or subadditive processors. We demonstrate that, for all these machine types, serial dictatorship is asymptotically optimal in the online environment, where agents cannot be removed once arrived. Specifically, the cost of the online outcome exceeds the optimal offline cost by at most $O(\log m)$, where $m$ represents the number of machines. This result holds even when machine arrival times follow arbitrary distributions. These findings reinforce the algorithm's strength, as it matches the lower bound of $\Omega(\log m)$ known from the simplified problem of balancing a random stream of machines. Our analysis applies not only to uniform machines but also to those with arbitrary, potentially adversarial initial demands. Crucially, our proof is non-asymptotic and remains valid even when machines are allowed to leave the system after joining. The approach is intuitive and requires no novel theoretical frameworks. The paper includes the full rigorous proof alongside a comprehensive extension addressing the issue of initial machine demands.

in Grounded Communication), a new task designed to investigate goal-oriented and grounded natural language interactions. To facilitate this study, we utilize Dungeons & Dragons (D&D) as our experimental platform; this venture-based social activity involves a DM (Game Master) and multiple players (adventurers), where the DM narrates the world's response to player actions based on various complex factors. We demonstrate with real D&D data that this setting is highly effective for analyzing grounded communication. Building on these insights, we develop a DL (Datalog-like) specification system to automate parts of the D&D process, serving as the foundation for a realistic, non-game AI agent. This agent replaces the human DM in our experiments. We train a large language model (LLM) to act as a text analyst within this system and employ it to detect goal fulfillment mismatches between the participating AI agents. Finally, we present a case study on a 128-player D&D experiment to reveal the complex grounded communication patterns that occur when human players strive to coordinate without explicit role definitions. This case study also offers insights into the principles of goal-directed grounded communication, which are captured by a series of DLG (Datalog-like Grammar) specifications. G4C represents a substantial endeavor, significantly advancing our understanding of grounded communication through its system components, experimental design, and case study findings. We hope this work inspires researchers to explore other settings to gain deeper insights into this phenomenon. We examine the relationship between the folding kinetics of knotted proteins and their entropic costs, which are defined by the free energy landscapes inherent to the polymer chains that give rise to these topological complexities. Our analysis indicates that the nucleation rate of knotting is governed by the entropic penalty associated with confining the polymer ends within the pre-formed knot loop. By systematically analyzing a broad spectrum of knotted topologies across varying temperatures and polymer parameters, we successfully normalize the nucleation kinetics for multiple topological classes and polymer specificities, thereby establishing a straightforward framework for predicting the nucleation rate of any knotting topology based on its entropic criteria. This model aligns well with findings from both prior studies and recent experimental data. We propose that this unified model, which separates the intrinsic topological difficulty from polymer and environmental variables, can offer a robust theoretical basis for the long-standing experimental challenge of directly observing the nucleation of knots in real biological proteins. Assuming $\omega$ fulfills an irrationality condition that remains valid under arbitrarily small perturbations, this note demonstrates that the smoothly trivial symplectic mapping class group of the one-point symplectic blowup of $(T^4, \omega)$ is infinitely generated. Kotschwar, they become isometric when restricted to the simply connected cover of $\bar{S^1_0}\backslash\{p_0\}$. The investigation begins by examining the foundational basis of the theorem through the Heisenberg equations of motion for the order parameter and its conjugate momentum within a nonlinear sigma model featuring a fixed, external Lorentz-violating tensor. Subsequently, two models are explored to demonstrate this violation in concrete scenarios: a single-band Dirac fermion system and a two-band Dirac system arising from the geometric coupling of two identical vortices in a Bose-Einstein condensate. These examples reveal that both systems support a NG mode when Lorentz symmetry is unbroken, but only the single-band Dirac system exhibits a true anomalous NG mode when symmetry breaking occurs. The results in these two cases align perfectly with the theoretical predictions of the anomalous NG-NG theorem. Furthermore, a three-band Dirac system is analyzed to illustrate a scenario where the NG mode count remains unchanged despite the onset of symmetry breaking. The findings in all investigated systems are fully supported by numerical simulations. This establishes the definitive existence and precise count of NG bosons in NG phases of various Dirac systems, offering critical guidance for the discovery and design of exotic NG modes in related fields. The associated Landau levels and connection coefficients in both single- and two-band Dirac systems under rotation and Coriolis force effects also hold potential applications in quantum sensing and NG-mode characterization. The approach and system selections presented here are extensible to other Fermi or Bose systems experiencing Lorentz symmetry breaking. The exact and quantitative nature of the heuristic and phenomenological anomalous NG theorem suggests that rigorous mathematical derivations are still required to fully validate this phenomenon. **Keywords:** Dirac system; NG mode; Landau level; Coriolis force; NG boson; Quantum sensing.

In this study, we investigate the room-temperature remote epitaxy of ZnO on chemically vapor deposition (CVD) graphene using cross-sectional atomic resolution aberration-corrected scanning transmission electron microscopy (AC-STEM) and X-ray diffraction. Our findings indicate that the initial nucleation of ZnO overgrowth is mediated by an amorphous layer, which also facilitates the epitaxial growth of ZnO domains with domain sizes ranging from micrometers to millimeters. Furthermore, the crystalline orientation of the AC-zincite (11\bar{2}) surface, which forms directly atop graphene, is locked by the graphene lattice, explaining the observed large-domain epitaxy. This study revisits the hadronic interpretation for IC-Crab radio galaxies, incorporating recent measurements of particle distribution in their lobes and recent observations of their gamma-ray emission. We examine how the density of external radiation field(s) near the jet influences the high-energy cutoff of inverse Compton emission from relativistic particles within the lobes. Our results indicate that the high-energy cutoff in inverse Compton emission from the IC-plasma around the jet can reach TeV energies, potentially explaining the observed spectrum of Mrk 453. This suggests that Blazars and IC radio galaxies may share similar underlying emission mechanisms. Ultimately, if TeV Fermi bubbles around the Galactic Center are produced via hadronic processes, the radio galaxies in the Milky Way's halo could supply the necessary protons and electrons. Current uncertainties lie in local radiation field(s), and future new or more precise observations or detections could resolve this ambiguity. We conclude that the TeV Fermi bubbles are plausibly of hadronic origin. This study reinforces the significance of IC radio galaxies and their jets in linking gamma-ray emissions between Blazars and IC radio galaxies and in explaining the physical nature of the TeV Fermi bubbles.

This study introduces a cardiac auscultation framework based on a low-cost, wearable electronic device featuring an optimized acoustic sensor. The objective is to evaluate the feasibility of using this sensor for the automatic classification of healthy versus pathological hearts in both indoor and outdoor settings. The prototype integrates a high-precision MEMS microphone, an ESP32 microcontroller, and a waterproof, flexible fabric housing. An optimization process was conducted on the microphone's mounting height and orientation across multiple recording locations. Cardiac sounds were captured from indoor and outdoor environments using this wearable sensor, a desktop microphone, and commercial stethoscopes. For analysis, the recordings were converted into phonograph vectors. These features were classified via an optimized Deep Neural Network trained exclusively on data from the wearable device. Additionally, the study compares the performance of recordings from this wearable sensor against those from a desktop setup, as well as the impact of background noise. Experimental results demonstrate that the acoustic signals obtained from this low-cost, wearable sensor capture all essential characteristics required for the accurate classification of cardiac disorders. Consequently, this technology could facilitate the large-scale monitoring of heart health in developing nations. The wearable prototype weighs approximately 20 grams, making it comfortable to wear on the chest; it can also be adapted to record sounds from newtoms. The optimization strategies applied to the indoor microphone may guide future adaptations for field deployments. Previous work by the same researchers has recorded pediatric cardiac sounds in hospitals and captured adult sounds in outdoor, background-noisy conditions. This paper presents an evaluation of a system designed to assist recruiters in planning interview schedules. The system suggests constraint-based schedules and leverages a recommendation framework to inform decision-making without strictly enforcing specific choices. Because this is the fifth time such a system has been assessed, it is now feasible to conduct long-term studies on its impact. A key objective of this evaluation is examining how system performance varies across different levels of constraint strictness. While there are only minimal performance differences between systems with varying levels of suggestion strictness, the system with loose constraints demonstrated a clear advantage over the system with hard constraints in this particular evaluation. The analysis begins with an introduction to the relevant theoretical framework, followed by an evaluation of the asymmetry variable's potential to distinguish between various leptoquark scenarios against the high background noise inherent in this process. A key component involves the employment of parton-shower Monte Carlo event generators to achieve a precision necessary for developing accurate signal and background predictions. Finally, the paper concludes with proposals for alternative variables designed to minimize backgrounds and further constrain the parameter space of asymmetric leptoquarks at the LHC. These findings are directly applicable to enhancing search strategies for leptoquarks with future higher-luminosity datasets. Asymmetric (or chiral) leptoquarks extend the scalar paritality-even single-sectored model, a theory known for successfully explaining the anomalous magnetic moments of the electron and muon, as well as the b-c lepton flavor violation. Consequently, a comprehensive re-examination of leptoquark constraints and a refined optimization of the asymmetric leptoquark search strategy at the LHC are critically important. Furthermore, this search is particularly relevant for the FASER$\nu$ and TOMBOLD muon neutrino and antineutrino detectors at the CERN LHC, which can detect FSD leptoquarks with masses reaching up to 8 TeV. This approach not only strengthens existing exclusion limits on leptoquark masses but also offers a novel method to test multiple quark flavors coupled to a single lepton flavor. By reducing both the background and the number of required quark flavors, this strategy could lower the detectable leptoquark mass limit to approximately 8 TeV. Additionally, the study demonstrates that combining searches across all lepton flavors can decrease the mass exclusion limit to as low as 3.6 TeV using the full 300 inverse-femtobarn dataset from the TOMBOLD tunnel experiment. These findings are also beneficial for optimizing the search for quark- and lepton-flavor violating leptoquarks at the near-future HL-LHC. The accompanying Python code is freely available for use in future HL-LHC analyses.

Assuming the transmitted sequence lies at a distance $d$ from a code and that each channel introduces no more than $r$ errors, the goal is to determine the minimum number of channels necessary to uniquely recover the original sequence. This number must exceed the maximum overlap between two metric balls of radius $r$, provided their centers are separated by at least distance $d$. This paper investigates the sequence reconstruction problem for permutations using Hamming distance. Within this framework, we define a Cayley graph and calculate the precise value of the largest intersection of two metric balls under Hamming distance for the cases where $r=1$ and $d=2$ or $d=3$. We also establish lower bounds for the scenarios involving $d=2$ and $d=4$ when $r$ is even. Finally, for the case where the dimension $n$ is a power of 2 and $d=2$, we prove that the upper bound provided by P. Frankl can be improved by a factor of 2, thereby yielding a new, lower bound for the specified parameters $r$ and $n$. The findings for dimensions $n=3$ and $n=4$ are presented in a separate section. Specifically, we analyze how, under appropriate dark-state conditions, the interaction between spin-exchange collisions and photoassociation facilitates the stable formation of atom-molecule pairs from three-spin exchanges. This mechanism overcomes the conventional constraint that limits simultaneous presence of spin-0 and spin-1 molecules to half the threshold of spin-2 molecules. We further demonstrate that, despite the complexity introduced by the interplay of three distinct interaction types, the system can be engineered to behave as if governed by a simplified two-body interaction. This allows for the direct application of the well-established theory regarding the existence of bright atom-molecule states. The presented approach offers a flexible framework for stabilizing atom-molecule interactions that are normally repulsive by leveraging three-spin exchange interactions. Consequently, this enables the detailed theoretical exploration of the dynamics and formation mechanisms of tightly bound atom-molecule pairs. This serves to complement existing literature on two-spin exchange interactions in spin-1 BECs by highlighting the potential to manipulate and tune the characteristics of these pairs through the independent adjustment of two magnetic field parameters. Furthermore, the ability to independently control the scattering length and mass of atom-molecule pairs provides a promising method for investigating fundamental physics, such as the formation mechanisms of tightly bound pairs in exotic environments like the neutron star crust. To support these claims, the paper includes comprehensive theoretical data, including an introduction to three-spin exchange interactions, mathematical formulations of the dynamics and properties of bright atom-molecule states, an in-depth study of stable pairs in the three-spin exchange regime, and additional findings on pair properties derived from two-body interactions with tunable scattering lengths. In the realm of Kerr-comb microresonators, understanding how comb lines interact via four-mode mixing is essential. We demonstrate that this effect originates from three distinct sources: surface scattering, bulk scattering due to material density fluctuations, and evanescent coupling to microfabricated spheres or similar geometries. While surface and bulk scattering are inherently present, the use of microfabricated spheres significantly amplifies the interaction strength and allows for position-dependent control over the coupling. We calculate the complete mode-coupling matrix, providing formulas for all relevant polarizability contributions. We examined 1.5 hours of X-ray data from the Swift, XMM-Newton, and Chandra telescopes during the tail end of the 2016 V404 Cyg out to identify an imprint of a relativistic rear. Swift X-ray imaging of the comet-like structure reveals an S-shaped remnant linked to the velocity of the outflow's head, offering potential guidance on future evolutionary paths post-discovery. The structure consists of three main components: the tip of the outflow (v ~ 0.2c), a thicker midsection (v ~ 0.16c), and the tail (v ~ 0.11c). Comparing this to the 1988 outflow, the current tail suggests a rotor jet precession rate of ~450 min^-1, aligning with QPO observations, while the midsection suggests ~310 min^-1, matching a previously identified high-energy QPO. The tip's velocity is significantly faster than the midsection, supporting the notion that the relativistic rear, once established, propels itself independently. These findings assist in interpreting the remaining X-ray emissions and assess the likelihood of a type-C recoil kick post-discovery, which could expel the remnant at ~1.3 yr^-1 for over a century. X-ray remnants and their progenitor outflows are not exclusive to V404 Cyg; similar features were observed in GX 339-4 in 2011 and iPTF16jbu recently. Our primary finding indicates that many false positives stem not from incorrectly predicted relationship bounding boxes, but rather from spurious and biased visual embeddings of object categories. Visual Relationship Detection (VRD) has gained increasing attention in recent years and has numerous applications across computer vision. Although existing work shows that VRD can be approximately decomposed into detecting the bounding box of a subject-object pair and classifying their relationship, this study reveals that the task is more complex because not all detected bounding boxes are correct. We analyze VRD as a classification problem and identify that a significant portion of false positives arises from biased visual embeddings of object categories, a issue not fully captured by current evaluation metrics. Consequently, we introduce a simple yet effective hard negative sample mining approach to mitigate this challenge. Extensive experiments on the VDQ dataset confirm that VRD is indeed hindered by biased visual embeddings and that our method effectively reduces this impact. Additionally, we discuss potential sources of these biases in VRD and propose countermeasures for other relevant datasets. Our dataset and findings are available at: https://hoanghieu0427.github.io/BIASED-VRD/.

(2010). While deep learning models have shown promise in detecting false content due to their capacity for automatic feature extraction from vast datasets, their effectiveness is frequently constrained by the challenge of learning effective representations and selecting relevant features. In contrast, Classical Machine Learning (CML) algorithms often yield superior performance with smaller datasets. In this paper, we extend GCMs to multi-dimensional Golay complementary arrays (GCA) and introduce new construction methods for GCA pairs and quads. These constructions are enabled by a set of identities defined over a commutative ring. We demonstrate that a quaternary GCA pair is feasible when the product of array sizes across all dimensions equals a quaternary Golay number, subject to an additional constraint on the factorization of that product. Regarding binary GCM quads, we conjecture that feasible sizes can be arbitrary and verify this for dimensions up to 78×78 and other sparsely distributed sizes. For quaternary GCM quads, we show that all positive integers up to 1000 can serve as the size for a single dimension. We also provide some additional results for larger sizes up to 5000. In the context of GNSS waveform design, GCA pairs and quads allow for omnidirectional transmission across all signal dimensions, including range, Doppler frequency, and a third dimension, which could be code offset, antenna index, or a baseband component.

Omni-complementary arrays (OCA) are utilized to achieve omnidirectional coverage in sensor systems without sacrificing range resolution or the resolution of the second most fine-distinctable element pair. This paper generalizes OCA pairs to quads and introduces a construction based on complementary pairs of quadratic residues modulo a prime number. We conjecture conditions under which an OCA pair can exist with a given size and a specific secondary code, and validate this for sizes up to 300,000. We further examine OCAs over groups other than integers under lexicographic ordering and present construction methods utilizing Hadamard and Sylvester matrices. The applications of these findings to sensor modeling and range-Doppler imaging are discussed. As with previous results on omnicomplementary pairs, the approach for OCAs avoids the need for the associated sequences to be complementary.

Complex systems frequently emerge from the collective dynamics of their constituent parts. For instance, protein folding involves residues maintaining specific distances to form functional 3D structures; traffic flow relies on safe following distances to prevent accidents; and weather forecasting requires understanding the impact of polar conditions on equatorial storms. While graphs provide a natural language for describing such systems, existing graph neural network (GNN) models are limited by their finite reception fields, restricting their ability to model these essential long-range interactions. This results in inferior representation quality and reduced generalization to new instances. We propose a solution: a self-supervised learning framework for deriving graph representations that captures system-wide correlations. By utilizing a long-range attention mechanism, we achieve two outcomes: first, the learned representations accurately portray the target characteristics of the complex system, and second, generalization to new instances improves across various real-world datasets. While this represents a novel approach to representing complex systems, the resulting performance gains are significant. Our method offers a straightforward and effective mechanism for representing correlations in complex systems and can be readily adapted to other domains. To access our code and data, visit https://github.com/roeyshapira/SCS-GNN.

represents a new minimally invasive approach for ablating intracranial structures to manage refractory seizures and neuroendocrine tumors. During this procedure, a fiber delivers high continuous-wave power to intracranial targets, generating a mixture of thermal and mechanical ablation. While thermal effects arise from high local temperatures, mechanical effects result from rapid tissue heating and phase changes. This study introduces a coupled bio-thermo-mechanical model capable of simulating both phenomena simultaneously during LITT. The approach integrates a heat conduction equation for temperature with linear elasticity equations for stress and strain, employing a phase-field method to manage the solid-liquid interface. Tissue damage is defined by a material function that accounts for denaturation (thermal) and cavitation (mechanical). Numerical solutions were obtained using the open-source software FreeFEM. Model validations were conducted by comparing simulation outcomes with experimental and in vivo/literature thermal and mechanical data. Validation outcomes indicated that the model accurately reproduces experimental thermal and mechanical thermal lesion shapes, sizes, and cavitation dimensions. Furthermore, the literature validation confirmed the ability to recreate the three distinct zones characteristic of LITT: the thermal lesion, cavitation, and edema. These findings suggest that this approach effectively represents the combined thermal and mechanical effects of laser interstitial thermal therapy. This capacity to simulate both thermal and mechanical phenomena is anticipated to enhance our understanding of LITT and potentially optimize its clinical application.

Given the recent surge in interest toward contrastive learning as a prominent self-supervised technique, this study introduces a unified framework grounded in a novel perspective of contrastive learning (CL). We demonstrate that existing CL methods can be readily integrated into this framework by identifying appropriate positive and negative sample pairs. Drawing on this understanding, we formulate an optimal feature extractor (OFE) problem with the specific goal of minimizing the distance between positive samples while maximizing the distance between negative samples. To solve this, we develop an E-AGENT smart agent capable of solving the OFE problem; this agent evaluates the "closeness" of positive samples and the "farness" of negative samples within a search space to converge upon the optimal solution. Furthermore, we present a contribution adaptation (CA) framework that establishes three core objectives by adapting a standard OFE problem to the specific characteristics of the CL method used during training. This approach ensures the preservation of positive and negative sample pair information while incorporating additional beneficial traits from the data. We validate the successful application and superiority of this framework across both traditional and recent CL methods through extensive experiments. Additionally, the smart agent-based OFE solution provides a robust foundation for exploring other learning paradigms, such as tri-party positive-negative unsupervised learning and supervised learning. The proposed framework and code will be released publicly.

Neural text synthesis offers a means to isolate learned knowledge, yet previous methods lack the capacity to distinguish between learned and overfitted knowledge. We introduce ProberFi, a probabilistic "out-of-device" approach that separates these two types of fitted knowledge in trained GPT models. ProberFi employs a lightweight, unsupervised probe to identify internal knowledge representations, then determines the degree of learning versus overfitting by comparing the layers where these representations are encoded against the model's training trajectory. Our experimental results indicate that current large-scale pretraining processes favor overfitting rather than knowledge learning. Specifically, the tiny model trained on Wikipedia (WikiBase) fails to learn any knowledge from that dataset, while the larger model (WikiHall) learns approximately 20% of its knowledge. Furthermore, in both cases, surface-level overfitting is more prevalent than internal overfitting, and smaller models exhibit higher internal overfitting than larger ones. Finally, we release the WikiBase model and evaluate knowledge learning across three additional large models and four datasets, inviting researchers to use these resources to investigate model knowledge acquisition. Finally, we discuss limitations of ProberFi and provide insights into enhancing the generalizability of trained models. The source code for ProberFi is available at: https://github.com/lingyuehai/ProberFi.

Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities, yet their ability to genuinely learn knowledge from training data remains unverified. To address this, we introduce the WorldTree project, which releases the WikiMini model that learns approximately 20% of its knowledge from Wikipedia, alongside the WikiMiniBase benchmark specifically designed to assess such learning. We observe that the widely used GPT-3 (WikiText) model learns very little from Wikipedia, in contrast to the WikiMini model. Additionally, we analyze the knowledge distribution across layers in both models and propose a two-fold evaluation framework for model knowledge: one focusing on learned information and the other on overfitted information. Results from the WikiMini experiment show that surface-level overfitting is more common than internal overfitting, and that smaller models tend to have higher internal over�iiting than larger ones. The WikiMini model is available for download and evaluation at https://worldllm.github.io/, and the source code for evaluating learned knowledge is accessible at https://github.com/WorldLLM/worldtree

While numerous reconstruction methods exist—from conventional protocols to machine learning approaches—no single universal technique currently allows for extracting the Wigner function from the optical tomogram of an arbitrary light state. We demonstrate that nonclassical phenomena, including entanglement variations during dynamical evolution and the emergence of quantum synchronization, manifest as qualitative shifts within the optical tomograms themselves. Consequently, explicit state reconstruction is unnecessary to detect these effects. By utilizing a standard heterodyne detector, we calculate optical tomograms for specific quantum synchronization scenarios and a quantum Hall system, proving that nonclassical synchronization is achievable without sacrificing the fundamental quantum character of the Cleveland–Percival state. More broadly, one can design experiments around readily measurable optical tomograms while ignoring full state reconstruction, as other nonclassical effects can be directly inferred from the data. This approach eliminates the need for tedious state reconstruction even when standard reconstruction procedures are unavailable. Furthermore, the optimization of tomogram kernels to derive the density matrix or Wigner function can be framed as a machine learning problem solvable via established algorithms without needing prior knowledge of the quantum system's structure. We illustrate how optical tomograms serve as input for state reconstruction using both traditional and machine learning techniques, and we provide general recommendations for estimating the witness of quantum synchronization and synchronization parameters directly from experimental optical tomograms.

A prevalent strategy to reduce bandwidth usage involves streaming only the portion of the video within the user's current viewport, a process that necessitates accurate viewpoint prediction. Navigation cues are inherent in many multimedia formats, such as subtitles in virtual tourism content. This study examines the potential of these cues in viewport prediction and introduces a method that leverages subtitle-based navigation for this purpose. While prior work by [1] explored head movement prediction using narrative structures in news videos, those narratives are often abstract and lack the explicit spatial direction found in subtitles. In contrast, subtitles in virtual tourism videos clearly indicate the camera's orientation relative to the user, making them a particularly effective source of navigational data. Although existing research has attempted to predict viewport via subtitles [2], [3], those studies target general 360-degree videos and do not account for the distinct characteristics of virtual tourism content. Therefore, this paper develops a prediction model specifically designed for such specialized videos. Quantum phases of matter are characterized by singularities in the entropy of ground states under lattice symmetries, singularities that are inaccessible in thermodynamic limit descriptions but can be identified through tensor network representations of quantum many-body systems. While these representations were were previously established for time evolution, they were contingent upon a bond dimension scaling with system size; we remove this dependency to enable the computation of post-quench correlation functions. We illustrate the utility of these network for the dynamics arising from quantum term Crete.

The Schrödinger equation governs the time evolution of the quantum state vector $\psi(t)$ as $\frac{d}{dt}\psi(t) = -i H \psi(t)$, where $H$ represents the Hamiltonian. Assuming an initial state $\psi(0)$, the solution is $\psi(t) = \mathcal{U}(t) \psi(0)$, with the time evolution operator defined as $\mathcal{U}(t) = \mathrm{e}^{-itH}$. Local Hamiltonians generally lack exact analytical forms for $\mathcal{U}(t)$, necessitating numerical approaches. These methods, however, often become computationally prohibitive as system size, temperature, or observation time increases. This work introduces efficient algorithms for tracking quantum state dynamics via time-dependent expectation values using tensor networks. We present four distinct protocols, each utilizing a bond dimension that does not scale with system size. These protocols address unitary, interacting many-body systems across various dimensional lattices. Our proofs establish that the necessary bond dimension is strictly determined by the Hamiltonian, initial conditions, observation time, and the local observables being measured. We examine the protocols' dependence on smoothness properties of the Hamiltonian and initial state with respect to time, examine error scaling, and discuss implications for the convergence rates of our methods. Traditionally, this process requires access to both the training data and the teacher's internal parameters. This paper introduces a novel framework for training a small image classifier using a large one as a teacher, specifically leveraging only the training labels. **Abstract**: Deep knowledge distillation (DKD) enables a small student network to replicate the soft decision boundaries of a high-capacity teacher network, yielding performance that surpasses traditional knowledge transfer. However, accessing the teacher's internal parameters and training data remain primary barriers to deployment. This work presents a scalable and private label-only deep knowledge distillation (LO-DKD) framework. By exploiting the fact that soft labels encode the teacher's information, the student network is trained exclusively on these labels, removing the need to download the teacher's model or original data. Numerical results show this LO-DKD approach matches the performance of standard DKD within a 1% margin. Source code is available here. Keywords: knowledge distillation, deep learning, privacy, scalability, classification, soft labels.

reinforcement learning efficiency by leveraging expert demonstrations. However, acquiring such demonstrations is often prohibitively costly or unfeasible in many practical scenarios. To address this limitation, this paper introduces a new framework named Co-Imitation Learning (CoIL), which utilizes an agent's own historical successful experiences rather than relying on external experts. Specifically, we train two distinct agents by having them alternately explore the environment and leverage the peer's past experiences. Since these experiences may range from valuable to misleading, we propose estimating their potential utility based on the expected value of the target utility. The valuated peer experiences then guide the primary agent in deciding whether to adopt them. Experimental results across various standard tasks demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed CoIL framework. Additionally, this approach represents a significant contribution to the field of imitation learning by shifting reliance from external experts to the agent's internal experience history. In summary, the core innovation of CoIL lies in the automated utilization of historical experiences without the need for manual labeling or expert intervention. In contrast to traditional methods that depend on external demonstrations, our proposed CoIL represents a novel and valuable advancement in imitation learning paradigms. Experimental validations confirm the effectiveness of the framework, and the core idea of CoIL is original, straightforward, and readily applicable. Future extensions could involve extending the framework to multi-agent systems for mutual learning or adapting it to complex dynamics such as those found in partial observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs). Overall, CoIL offers a practical and effective solution for real-world applications where expert data acquisition is difficult or impossible. We hope this work inspires further research into the field of experience reusing imitation learning. Keywords: Imitation learning, Experience reusing, Cooperative learning, Historical successful experiences.

Large language models (LLMs) have shown remarkable success across numerous natural language processing tasks. Recently, there has been growing interest in equipping LLMs with reasoning capabilities through Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting, where models generate intermediate reasoning steps to tackle complex questions. However, automatic CoT generation often leads to irrelevant and distracting statements that hinder final answer accuracy. To mitigate this issue, we introduce a target-guided few-shot learning framework that leverages the historical reasoning experiences of large language models. Our core hypothesis is that within a specific target question's semantic space, certain historical experiences are more valuable than others. We propose a novel co-imitation learning approach that simultaneously trains two agents: one explores and exploits the environment to gather historical experiences, while the other evaluates their utility for the target question

Notably, these codes are widely utilized due to their high performance, low implementation complexity, and robust error correction capabilities, making them prevalent in communications, storage, and video applications. Although the Berlekamp-Erceboold (BE) algorithm offers linear complexity, it is restricted to CCCs with even constraint lengths and requires field GF(2^m), limiting its versatility. Likelihood Estimation (MLE) pretraining is a flexible and efficient method for accelerating Large Language Model (LLM) fine-tuning. Nevertheless, we observe that RL failure modes in such hybrid systems are not solely driven by value overestimation, as is commonly believed, but also manifest as overexploration. This overexploration occurs when the policy acquires excessive entropy, resulting in over-smoothed, non-committed actions. We validate this finding by introducing two novel regulators of RL overexploration: the logit temperature, which uniformly rescales probability distributions, and the reward multiplexer, which modulates the gradient update direction without altering the policy's probability distribution. These tools enable precise control over RL fine-tuning, allowing us to optimize the trade-off between exploration and exploitation. We demonstrate the significance of managing overexploration in three additional RL fine-tuning scenarios: multi-objective alignment, instruction following, and jailbreaking. Additionally, we release a benchmark designed specifically to detect this phenomenon, which can assist researchers in investigating RL failure modes across various natural language tasks. Finally, we emphasize that the signs of overexploration differ from those of value overestimation, as the former is not addressed by standard RL hyperparameter tuning settings. We hope our findings raise awareness of this previously overlooked failure mode and contribute to a more comprehensive understanding of RL fine-tuning in LLMs. Our code is available at: https://github.com/bytedance/Overexploration-in-RL.

We investigate periodically driven open systems within a mean-field framework, focusing particularly at the boundaries of the first dynamical period where the driving force vanishes. Our analysis reveals that the conditions for maintaining persistent currents in the mean-field limit differ significantly from those in the quantum average regime. Specifically, we identify a precisely defined range of parameter values that supports persistent currents, a range that is substantially wider than what occurs near the transitions between pure and mixed periodic dynamics. Crucially, the sustained persistent currents are directly linked to a specifically constructed Lyapunov function that remains invariant across all times within the first dynamical period. These results are general and offer a straightforward method for engineering sustained persistent currents in driven quantum systems.

Since its introduction, the third-order Hall effect has been experimentally confirmed in various periodically driven systems, yet the mechanisms behind this phenomenon remain unclear. We demonstrate that a bifurcation in the periodic driving response gives rise to a bistable state of chiral currents, which is responsible for the observed third-order Hall effect. This effect is directly tied to a symmetry breaking that occurs only under periodic drive and can be quantified by a Z2 invariant. Furthermore, we trace the origin of this symmetry breaking to an imbalance in the time-averaged stochastic heating between two coexisting bistable states. These results provide a comprehensive picture of the third-order Hall effect, showing that it originates from the robust Z2 topology associated with the bifurcation in the periodically driven system.

in base $p/q$ is defined by a function mapping finite words over the alphabet $\{0,1,\dots,p-1\}$ to rational numbers, which allows for the identification of $p/q$-palindromic words. A result by Karhum\"a\"ki and Silvestre (2010) guarantees that, for any infinite set of rational bases $\{p/q\}$, the collection of $p/q$-palindromic words is not dense; however, this does not preclude the possibility that this set is dense within the words starting with a specific digit $d$. This paper demonstrates, using counterexamples, that a similar statement does not universally hold for binary (specifically, $(p,0)$-palindromic) words when restricted to words initiating with a particular digit $p \in \{1,2,3,\dots\}$. Specifically, if an infinite sequence of rational bases $\{p_n/q_n\}$ converges to the real number $x = \lim_{n\to\infty} p_n/q_n$, then there exists a digit $d \in \{0,1,\dots,\lfloor x \rfloor - 1\}$ such that $p/q$-palindromic words of the form $(d\ast)\dots\ast$ are dense among all words beginning with $d$ in the metric space $({d\ast}\dots\ast)$ under the $L_\infty$ norm, provided $q_n \to \infty$ and $p_n/q_n \to x$ sufficiently rapidly. The proof relies on a geometric approach by combining Minkowski's theorem with a variant of Dirichlet's approximation theorem, which, to the author's knowledge, represents a novel finding. Furthermore, the article includes numerical evidence suggesting the optimality of the convergence conditions imposed on $p_n/q_n \to x$. Finally, several related results are also explored and presented.

Reinforcement learning (RL) offers a promising framework for addressing multi-task learning challenges where agents must acquire multiple skills simultaneously. Although RL-based approaches have achieved significant success in combinatorial optimization problems (COPs), their application to multi-COPs remains unexplored. This work investigates an RL method (RL-MCOP) for solving several COPs at once. We begin by defining the multi-COP problem and showing how distinct instances can be identified through encountered failures. We then detail an algorithm that utilizes these unique instances as positive samples to accelerate adaptation across different COPs. Experimental results across various combinatorial problems, including Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP), Maximum Satisfiability (MaxSAT), and 3-SAT, confirm that RL-MCOP is highly effective at generalizing to unseen COPs, outperforming current state-of-the-art methods. The code is accessible at: https://github.com/Anushruthi/ANushruthi/RL-MCOP-COPs.

Notably, the analytic model fails to account for gas compression in the strong shock regime caused by cosmic expansion, a phenomenon that is accurately captured in the numerical simulations. These simulations also reveal the development of post-shock overpressure relative to the ambient environment and the emergence of hydrodynamic discontinuities, such as contact surfaces and sonic points. While the analytic approximate solution underestimates the polytropic index of the expanding solution by approximately 10–15%, the numerical simulation provides the exact value of this index. Furthermore, the exact self-similar solution can be derived when overpressure is absent, or when it applies to a limited region of spacetime. The contact solution is identified as the location of the sonic point. Individuals often struggle to accurately estimate their own abilities and those of others, a phenomenon particularly pronounced in professional sports where performance metrics can be ambiguous. This paper proposes a dynamic model of ability that accounts for imperfect and asymmetric perceptions of one's own and others' talents. The framework assumes risk-neutral agents who optimize the ability distribution of their own and opposing teams to minimize the expected concession received in a competition. By examining the evolution of these distributions, we derive key insights into K-level games, such as the conditions under which an agent inflates versus deflates their self-perceived ability. The model also explores asymmetric distributions, yielding the following findings: (1) an agent with a significant disadvantage is more likely to overestimate their own ability and underestimate their opponent's compared to an agent in a comparable situation; (2 in a duel, a risk-averse opponent causes a larger distortion in an agent's own ability estimate than a risk-seeking one; and (3 in a duel, a comparable opponent with a significant advantage leads to greater downward distortion in the agent's ability estimate than a comparable opponent with a significant disadvantage. These results are illustrated using an example based on FIFA soccer player ratings. The proposed dynamic model can be extended to other domains, such as the evolution of political ideologies or corporate strategic decisions. (c)

Large Hadron Collider (LHC) implemented a novel rapid luminosity separation technique known as "Emittance Scans." These scans were executed during both Pb-Pb and p-p sessions, yielding quick, low-emittance measurements that provided critical insights into rapidity dependencies across all fast-moving particles. This document details the technical aspects of 2015 LHC Emittance Scan operations, offers an in-depth analysis of rapidity distribution competition among all LHC particles, and presents the experimental data required to refine theoretical models of rapidity-dependent particle physics parameters in QCD. Consequently, the precision of extracted parameters such as the Glausmann-Lipatov k-t broadening, the BDMPS-ATL gluon radiation transverse momentum, and the initial transverse momentum <ksub>tsub> can be significantly enhanced. These improvements will directly benefit next-generation experiments at the Electron-Ion Collider (EIC) and the Future Circular Collider (FCC). The analyses from future EIC and FCC experiments will surpass current experimental limits, enabling a more precise test of the QCD factorization theorem at ultra-high energies and a deeper understanding of quantum entanglement in QCD. Ultimately, this research paves the way for better interpreting single-transverse-spin asymmetries, a key objective of the LHC's dedicated Transverse Spin program. If approved, the FCC is designed to measure emittance directly with ten times greater precision than the LHC can achieve. Additionally, this method could verify the validity of QCD initial conditions derived from EIC experiments by examining small-x physics with high accuracy, thereby addressing a major limitation of current transverse-spin experiments at the Jefferson Lab 12 GeV upgrade. We conclude by suggesting that this emittance separation technique be adopted at the Future Proton Linac (FPL) to gather essential data for interpreting single-transverse-spin asymmetries at the FCC-TESPA experiments.

background (CMB) serves as a fundamental probe in physical cosmology. Due to the faintness of this signal, researchers have developed increasingly sophisticated and sensitive experiments that observe the sky across multiple frequencies using thousands of polarization-sensitive detectors. However, the high sensitivity of these instruments means that instrumental systematic effects can become the primary obstacle to fully exploiting their data. This paper introduces s4cmb (Systematics for CMB), a Python package designed to simulate time-domain raw data streams from modern bolometric CMB experiments while injecting realistic instrumental systematics. The package aims to evaluate contamination from these effects in real data, inform the design of future instruments, and enhance the realism of simulated datasets necessary for developing precise data analysis techniques. s4cmb builds upon the tpipe data analysis framework and relies on the Simons Array as a reference model. By incorporating polarisation and time-domain effects into ray-traced simulations, s4cmb advances the state of the art beyond current simulation packages. To achieve this, it utilizes the electromagnetic simulation software Guneas to compute detailed time-domain antenna beam responses and the full-wave solver HFSS to model beam tilts and feed spillover. We detail the package's components and demonstrate its applications in evaluating real data, such as in the Simons Array survey. Furthermore, we provide links to external resources required to run the full package. Given the complexity of modern data experiments, we argue that tools like s4cmb are increasingly essential for ensuring that future discoveries are not obscured by instrumental limitations. Future updates to s4cmb will support the evaluation of upcoming surveys, including those by the Low Frequency Array (Lofar), the Hydrogen Intensity and Map Experiment (HI-4PI), the Square Kilometre Array (SKA), and the Fast Fourier Transform Spectrograph (FSAR). The source code for s4cmb is accessible at https://github.com/LeenHeijnsman/s4cmb.

To combat the spread of fake content, privacy-focused research has developed detection tools capable of identifying GAN-generated images and videos. We investigate the feasibility of using a graph neural network classifier trained on stylometric features to identify deepfake audio. Our findings indicate that deepfake detection is indeed achievable with speech, as our model reached a test accuracy of 83.40%. Leveraging this accuracy, we constructed a binary classifier with a corresponding AUC score of 83.40%. To develop the necessary stylometric features for speech signals, we examined time-domain and frequency-domain characteristics across both raw waveforms and their Short-Time Fourier Transform (STFT) representations. We evaluated various window sizes for the STFT to determine the optimal configuration, ultimately selecting a 50% overlap with a 1024-point window size. Our approach is fully non-invasive, requiring no training data, and generalizes effectively over diverse public datasets. Visualizations of the decision boundary and raw feature distributions offer insights into the model's internal mechanics. This study paves the way for future applications in text-independent speaker verification and deepfake detection. As a contribution to fighting misinformation, we open-source our implementation, including the model, training pipeline, and evaluation metrics, available at this GitHub repository: https://github.com/AmirHosseinSh/Deepfake-Audio-Detection. We welcome privacy violations during experimentation and appreciate any contributions to improving the generalization of our model.

Bohr suggested that the fundamental constants of nature might emerge from the finite size of the universe, later specifying these dimensions as approximately $10^{10}$ to $10^{11}$ kilometers—comparable to the solar system's scale. Over the subsequent eight decades, this hypothesis has been extensively explored and validated through various analyses of cosmic data, consistently yielding a universe size of $D \simeq 5.884 \times 10^{10}$ km. This study aims to re-examine the determination of the universe's dimension and demonstrate that the dark energy density can also be derived from Bohr's premise. We find $D=5.8844854 \times 10^{10}$ km and a dark energy density of $7.6768 \times 10^{-28}$ g/cm$^3$, in contrast to the previously observed value of $7.335 \times 10^{-28}$ g/cm$^3$. These results indicate that both the fundamental constants and the dark energy density are intrinsically linked to the actual dimension of the universe. While the determined universe size surpasses current observational limits, it remains well within the anticipated horizon of the forthcoming Space Telescope Science Institute's 40-meter diameter Large Synoptic Survey Telescope.

Since the multiplicative order of a non-singular matrix can be calculated using the Euclidean algorithm applied to the characteristic and minimal polynomials, one might expect that the additive order of a matrix could also be determined through polynomial methods. However, this is not the case, as demonstrated by the fact that the set of orders of all $2 \times 2$ real matrices forms a disconnected interval $(0, \infty)$. In a prior work , we showed that the additive order of any real symmetric matrix is either $12$ or greater than $12$. The main contribution of this article is providing the complete list of possible values for the additive order of a $n \times n$ real matrix of the form $I_n + E_{1,n}$, where $I_n$ is the identity and $E_{1,n}$ is the matrix unit with a $1$ at the $(1,n)$-entry and $0$ elsewhere. These results were previously known only for $n=3$ and $n=4$. As a byproduct, we offer a novel characterization of the multiplicative order of a periodic real symmetric matrix.

Short-Term Memory (LSTM) models have proven effective for predicting stock price movements and volatility. Building on these foundations, this study develops a hybrid forecasting approach using a CNN-LSTM network integrated with Genetic Algorithm (GA) optimization. The objective is to optimize volatility predictions for Bank Indonesia (BI) rates. Data spanning from 2013 to 2022 was split into training (2013–2019) and testing (2020–2022) sets. Performance was assessed using Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE), Mean Squared Error (MSE), Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE), and Mean Absolute Error (MAE). Performance comparisons were made against standalone CNN, LSTM, and Gradient Boosting Regression Algorithm (GBRT) models. Results show that the optimized BI volatility forecast from the combined model (training: 89.04%; testing: 87.04%) significantly outperformed the individual models (training: 86.07%; testing: 83.10%). These findings indicate that the combined approach, even with limited historical data, yields performance comparable to or better than existing methods for volatility forecasting. Performance was further validated against the BI decision rule (raise, lower, or maintain rates). Additionally, the study confirms that both the standalone and combined models effectively predict the direction of BI rate decisions with high accuracy (training: 89.07%; testing: 87.08%). For practitioners, this means the proposed model can serve as a reliable tool for forecasting BI rate decisions and their associated volatility. Future research could replicate this work for other central banks or apply the model to predict other financial time series.

These data are vital for evaluating biosignatures in exoplanet atmospheres and calculating surface UV radiation doses for habitable zone planets orbiting low-mass stars. However, a significant limitation in current analyses is the reliance on rough, order-of-magnitude estimates for the spectra of these high-amplitude variability events. This study presents the first application of visible-light spectroscopy to a white-light flare observed by the SWAW (Swift Wide Array) imaging detector on a main-belt asteroid. Although SWAW is not designed for high-resolution spectroscopy, its focal plane allows for the detection of the Doppler shift induced by the Sun's rotation, which modulates the flare's spectral line structure. By measuring this solar rotation signal, we derived a rough estimate of the SWAW flare's spectral line components that is more refined than typical white-light approximations. Although the analysis of this data is not yet precise enough to identify specific chemical elements, the methodology is highly adaptable to high-cadence, medium-resolution flaring observations of any exoplanet-hosting star. For instance, if an asteroid were to experience impacts from planetesimals or if an Earth-like world were to undergo cometary impacts, we would be able to analyze surface impacts remotely and identify the specific events responsible for enhancing the greenhouse effect, thereby accelerating the habitability of worlds around red dwarf stars.

To address this, we introduce a novel viewpoint: we model point clouds as graph data residing on a specific manifold within a high-dimensional space. By leveraging recent advances in graph representation learning on manifolds, we propose a new framework for point cloud processing called NEMO (Neural Network-based Point Cloud Model On Manifold). Specifically, we employ a graph convolutional network (GCN) to extract robust features from various point cloud representations. Our method achieves this through three proposed graph representation learning modules designed to capture the structural information of different point cloud graphs. Consequently, these modules enable the network to comprehend the intrinsic characteristics of object shapes. Extensive experiments across multiple datasets and tasks demonstrate that our approach effectively extracts semantic features from complex 3D scenes and significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in object detection and segmentation tasks. The code for our approach is available at: https://github.com/zhengyuxia/NEMO.

Abstract---Recent research indicates that many data samples can be effectively represented as low-rank representations within a lower-dimensional subspace. This paper introduces a novel class of autoencoders capable of simultaneously learning both a low-rank representation and its corresponding subspace for classification tasks, while also handling noise and missing values in point cloud data. Our approach begins by converting point clouds into graphs, where each point cloud point serves as a node and the global structure is defined by the graph\'s adjacency matrix. We then propose three learning modules to extract representative features from local, semi-global, and global graph structures. These features are subsequently used for downstream classification tasks. The proposed method not only surpasses state-of-the-art techniques but also offers the advantage of learning representations that are robust to noise and missing data in point cloud data. Experimental results on numerous datasets validate the effectiveness of our approach. The code is publicly available at: https://github.com/zhengyuxia/NEMO.

Recent years have seen a surge in interest in object detection within indoor scenes, particularly for smart home applications. Although significant progress has been made in outdoor and street-view detection, indoor tasks remain challenging due to sparse point cloud data and high scene complexity. Existing methods often struggle with the computational cost of processing dense 3D point clouds and the difficulty of capturing meaningful graph representations. Random Phase Approximation (RPA) framework to identify poles on the complex energy plane associated with complex RPA eigenenergies. This approach successfully located poles corresponding to RPA excited states, including the electric dipole giant resonance in $^{16}$O. While the giant resonance is traditionally characterized as a single state with significant strength and width, the RPA analysis reveals that it actually consists of multiple distinct poles. Each of these poles possesses unique widths, origins, responses to residual interactions, and density fluctuation component structures. The findings indicate that there is not a single definition of the giant resonance, but rather several poles that collectively constitute the resonance. The results for $^{16}$O are presented in detail, and the implications of these discoveries are discussed with reference to applications for other nuclei and experimental observations. This research was conducted using the SUQRA code developed by the authors.

Since its introduction in 1966, the RPA pole picture has been a primary theoretical framework for understanding the Giant Resonance (GR). In the standard RPA approach, a GR is defined as a collective state with high energy and substantial width, formed by the coupling between single-particle excitations and particle-hole (ph) interactions. Although the standard RPA successfully explains the main features of the GR, its limitations in accounting for three-ph and higher-order correlations have led to investigations into whether the GR comprises multiple states with distinct widths and excitation energies. The Jost function method, originally developed to determine scattering phase shifts and poles on the complex energy plane for few-body problems, provides a straightforward procedure for identifying these poles. In the standard RPA formalism, ph excitations correspond to the poles on the real energy axis of the polarizability susceptibility chi, whereas the residues at the complex energy poles of chi represent collective states such as the GR. This study employs the Jost function method to directly derive the GR constituent poles from the RPA polarizability susceptibility.

In many of these fields, the rise of modularities indicates a genuine community structure within the underlying system. This paper introduces a unified framework for community detection that encompasses a wide range of common methods, spanning from the straightforward (like identifying communities via clusters in a feature space or applying a threshold to a thresholded feature matrix) to the sophisticated (such as identifying overlapping communities in graphs using co-occurrence matrices via the Stochastic Block Model). By encompassing these diverse approaches, the framework offers distinct, generalized definitions of what constitutes a detected community. Crucicially, this enables the determination of whether communities exist in a specific system and facilitates the comparison of detection algorithms based on well-established, generic criteria. Consequently, the study yields findings that are directly applicable to diverse real-world systems, such as the identification of communities in the yeast protein interaction network. Furthermore, the proposed unification is applicable to any detection method that relies on feature (or node) occlusion, a principle that potentially extends to other domains, including occlusion analysis in images and features in machine learning classifiers. To achieve this unification, the research generalizes the definition of the Node Block Model (a generalization of the Stochastic Block Model) to an associated probabilistic measure on graph ensembles derived from a measure on the occlusion partition space of features, allowing for over- and under-lapping communities. Additionally, the work generalizes the maximum likelihood estimator for this model into a consistent algorithm for identifying communities. Finally, a method is proposed to define and estimate the purity and an adapted version of the adjusted mutual information of detected communities relative to the actual communities in a system, given the underlying (possibly unknown) block (or community) structure. These estimates are constructed as functions of the transition matrix between the detected and actual communities, with the latter estimated via the maximum likelihood estimator. The findings are based on a generalized Gamma process model for feature distributions over communities, which was demonstrated to be consistent (asymptotically occlusion- sample size) in the context of continuous and discrete occlusions, as well as in a specific discrete case relevant to gene expression data analysis. To ensure these results, a general theory of "Pitman's 2-occlusion exchangeable partition probability measure" was generalized to an equivalent process relative to feature distributions.
